choices.text: Every mutation harms the organism, because any change to DNA breaks a protein
Mutations are harmful only in body cells, never in gametes
Most mutations are neutral: only some are harmful, and a rare few are beneficial
Mutations never affect the organism at all

questions.explanation: The trap claim is: Every mutation harms the organism. Most mutations are neutral: only some are harmful, and a rare few are the raw material of evolution. A changed base may leave the amino acid - and the protein's job - unchanged, as in scene s5.
questions.prompt: A student says every change to a DNA sequence must damage the organism. What is correct?

questions.explanation: The Punnett square in scene s2 gives AA, Aa, Aa and aa: only the aa box (1 in 4) shows the recessive trait, while 3 in 4 show the dominant trait.
questions.prompt: Two heterozygous parents (Aa x Aa) have a child. What is the probability the child shows the recessive trait?

questions.answer: DNA is transcribed into mRNA in the nucleus, and the mRNA is translated into a polypeptide at a ribosome in the cytoplasm.
questions.explanation: Scene s1 shows the one-way flow: transcription copies DNA into mRNA in the nucleus, then translation reads the mRNA at a ribosome to build the polypeptide chain.
questions.prompt: Outline the central dogma in one or two sentences, naming where transcription and translation happen.

questions.answer: A son has only one X chromosome, so the recessive h allele has no second allele to mask it and the trait shows; a daughter has a second X carrying H, which masks h, so she is a carrier without symptoms.
questions.explanation: Scene s4 makes the asymmetry explicit: sons receive their only X from their mother and a Y from their father, so there is no second X to mask a recessive allele; daughters receive an X from each parent.
questions.prompt: A carrier mother (X^H X^h) and a normal father (X^H Y) have children. Explain why a son who inherits X^h has haemophilia, while a daughter who inherits X^h usually does not.

questions.explanation: Independent assortment in scene s3 gives sixteen equally likely boxes in four phenotype classes: 9 both dominants, 3 and 3 for the mixed classes, and 1 double recessive - the 9:3:3:1 ratio.
questions.prompt: A dihybrid cross between two double heterozygotes (RrYy x RrYy), with the genes on different chromosomes, produces offspring. What is the expected phenotype ratio?
